source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Phosphorus is present in the soil and in the corn plant in smaller quantities compared to nitrogen and potassium, but it is still very important for corn production. Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus is not easily lost through volatilization, wind, or runoff, and its mobility within the soil is very low (near-immobile). Corn absorbs phosphorus from the soil in dissolved ionic forms, regardless of whether it originates from chemical or organic fertilizer. If phosphorus is deficient, symptoms typically appear before the plant reaches about 0.7 meters in height.

Symptoms of phosphorus deficiency: poor overall growth, with stunting in severe cases; young leaves appear dull green while older leaves take on a purplish color; in some varieties the leaves show purple or reddish coloring; and yield drops sharply because ears are small — in severe cases, no ear or grain forms at all.

Causes of phosphorus deficiency include: soil with high untreated organic-matter content, insufficient phosphorus applied at planting, cold weather, acidic soil, and iron-rich soil.

Correction: select a fertilizer with a high phosphorus content and apply it before or during planting (see the basal-fertilizer entry in this dataset for the DAP nutrient figures, which contain a genuine numeric discrepancy in the source between 46% and 48% phosphorus). Because phosphorus has very low mobility in soil, it should be placed close to the seed/planting row so the crop's roots can reach it. Continuous, repeated DAP use can increase soil acidity. Corn residue (stalks) is rich in phosphorus, so ploughing residue back into the soil is recommended as a way to build up soil fertility.
